content.title: 10 Principles of Good Web Design
content.summary: Ten practical checks for a website that explains your offer, helps people choose and gives them a clear next step.
content.body:
A website review is more useful when it starts with a visitor task. Pick one: find a suitable product, understand a service or send an enquiry. Then follow that task on your own site, including on a phone. These ten checks give your team a concrete way to discuss what needs work.

1. Explain the offer first

The opening screen should tell people what you offer and who it is for. Pair the headline with a relevant product or work example. A striking image cannot carry an unclear offer on its own.

2. Give each page a next step

Choose a main action that follows naturally from the content: explore a range, see a case study or discuss a project. Keep secondary options available without making every button compete equally.

3. Use navigation your customers understand

Organise pages around familiar products, services and questions. Test the labels with someone who has not worked on the site. If they need an explanation, the navigation may need simpler language.

4. Design with the real content

Use actual product names, long titles, variants and photographs early. Sample content can hide the very layout problems that appear when the full catalogue arrives.

5. Make choices easy to compare

Keep recurring information in consistent positions. On a product range, that might mean size, flavour and price. For services, show fit, scope and the next step using the same structure.

6. Review the mobile sequence

A desktop grid becomes a reading order on a phone. Make sure the important offer and proof arrive before repeated explanations. Check that images still show the product rather than an accidental crop.

7. Keep interaction accessible

Use readable contrast, clear labels and visible keyboard focus. Test menus, filters and forms without a mouse. Motion should leave the content understandable when it is paused or reduced.

8. Show genuine proof

Use real work and explain your contribution. A design concept, a launched store and a campaign asset are different kinds of evidence. Label them clearly and avoid implying results you have not measured.

9. Test the whole enquiry

Do more than click the submit button. Check required-field messages, a successful receipt and what happens when delivery fails. Visitors should keep their details if something goes wrong.

10. Agree how to judge the change

Define the action that matters before redesigning. A calendar click is not a booked call, and a form start is not a qualified enquiry. Where measurement is available, compare those outcomes separately.

Look at the decisions in context

The BPM website design connects a colour-coded product range with its page layouts. It is an example of design choices supporting product discovery, not a claim of a measured sales uplift. Use the case below to discuss how similar decisions could apply to your own range.

article:mastering-illustration-styles-in.label: Mastering Illustration Styles in Graphic Design

content.title: Choosing illustration for your product brand
content.summary: Choose illustration around what your product brand needs to communicate, where the artwork will appear and how your team will use it.
content.body:
Choosing an illustration style is a brand decision before it is a matter of taste. A playful character, a detailed ingredient drawing and a simple graphic symbol each do a different job. Start by naming the job your artwork needs to do.

Decide what the image should explain

Is it helping customers recognise a flavour, understand how to use a product or connect with the brand’s personality? One image does not need to do all three. Agree the priority before collecting references.

Choose a visual language with a purpose

  • Simple line work: useful when the composition needs small, repeatable symbols or supporting details.
  • Bold graphic shapes: worth exploring when the identity depends on colour and a recognisable silhouette.
  • Character-led artwork: a direction to consider when expression and storytelling are central to the brand.
  • Detailed drawings: can make room for ingredients, craft or a more descriptive product story.

These are starting points for exploration. Review examples beside your typography, colour palette and product photography before choosing.

Test the smallest application

Put a draft on the actual pack size and in a mobile product card. Details that look appealing on a large presentation may disappear at a small scale. Discuss line weight, contrast and reproduction with the designer and production partner.

Plan a family, not one isolated picture

If several variants need artwork, define the shared rules: viewpoint, proportions, colour use and level of detail. Decide how a future product can join the range without looking like it belongs to another brand.

Give the designer a useful brief

  • The audience and the idea the illustration should communicate.
  • Brand files and examples of existing applications.
  • Formats, dimensions and production constraints.
  • The number of artworks and variants needed.
  • Where the finished work will be used, including any licensing requirements to agree.

Review it as part of the system

Look at the illustration alongside the product name, information hierarchy and other brand elements. The goal is a coherent presentation. Marin’s project is a useful place to explore how graphic elements, colour and type can share a recognisable direction across applications.

article:brand-designer-what-is-it-and-ho.label: Brand Designer: What Is It? and How to Become One?

content.title: What does a brand designer do?
content.summary: How brand designers turn a business direction into an identity, and the skills to practise if you want to do that work.
content.body:
A brand designer creates the visual identity a business uses to present itself. That can include a logo, colours, typography, illustrations and layouts. The work starts with understanding the business and its customers, then deciding what the design needs to communicate.

Start with the brief

A useful brief explains the offer, audience and problem. Is the business launching, entering a new market or working with an identity that has become difficult to use? The designer needs that context before choosing a visual direction.

Design a system, not only a logo

The logo is one part of an identity. Type, colour, imagery and layout need to work together on the applications the business uses. Test the direction on a real product pack, website page or sales document. Those examples reveal whether the identity is useful beyond the presentation.

Explain the decisions

A designer should be able to explain why a direction fits the brief. Connect your choices to what customers need to recognise or understand. Invite feedback on those decisions, then refine the work through the agreed review stages.

Prepare the handoff

Agree which files and applications the client needs. Organise them clearly and include guidance on using the identity. A team needs to know which logo version to choose, how to use the colours and typography, and where to find the final artwork.

If you want to become a brand designer

Practise typography, composition, colour and visual research alongside the software. Create projects around specific briefs and show the decisions behind the work. Label self-initiated concepts clearly, seek feedback and refine your portfolio. A useful case study explains the problem, your role and how the identity works in context.

See an identity across its applications

Our CocoFro work shows an identity carried across a family of product packs. Look at which elements stay consistent and which change between flavours. That relationship between a shared system and individual products is part of a brand designer’s job.

article:beautiful-responsive-websites-ma.label: Is Strikingly Right for Your Website?

content.title: Is Strikingly Right for Your Website?
content.summary: A practical review of Strikingly for a small site: use real content, check the mobile layout and test the journey before publishing.
content.body:
Strikingly can be a useful starting point for a small website, but a responsive template is only the beginning. Before choosing a platform, write down what visitors need to do: understand the offer, compare services or products, and reach you. Then build one representative page with your real content.

Test the content in the layout

Try your longest heading, actual product or service names, and the photographs you intend to use. A demo page can look balanced while the real copy wraps awkwardly or the key subject disappears in a mobile crop. Review the first screen and the full page on a phone.

Check the mobile editing workflow

Strikingly provides a phone view in its editor. Its help centre says changes made in that view also affect the desktop site. The separate phone app can edit and manage sites, but some sections and settings still require desktop editing. Plan to review both layouts after every significant change rather than assuming one preview covers the other.

Walk through the whole visitor task

  • Can a new visitor tell what the business offers?
  • Are navigation labels, buttons and form fields clear on a small screen?
  • Do images show the product or work without an accidental crop?
  • Does the enquiry or purchase path work from start to finish?

If the site needs complex store behaviour or custom integrations, list those requirements before committing to a template. The best fit depends on the content, maintenance needs and the action customers should take.

Review Strikingly’s mobile editor guidance and phone editing limits for current product details.

article:ashbi-creative-studio-has-been-f.label: Ashbi Creative Studio Has Been Featured On Safety Detectives

content.title: Ashbi’s website security interview with SafetyDetectives
content.summary: Cameron discusses website security and running a creative studio in an interview with SafetyDetectives.
content.body:
Read the original SafetyDetectives interview.

SafetyDetectives spoke with Cameron Ashley co-founder of Ashbi Creative Studios. We discussed tips and strategies for businesses on how to secure their website and protect it from hackers, and what to do if your site gets hacked.

HI CAMERON, CAN YOU TELL ME A LITTLE BIT ABOUT YOUR PROFESSIONAL BACKGROUND? HOW LONG HAVE YOU BEEN AT ASHBI CREATIVE STUDIOS?

I’ve worked professionally in the IT industry for 10 years at a large organization and now am the head operations director at my own start-up company, Ashbi Creative Studio. Along with my partner, we provide content marketing and design services to companies looking to use new digital marketing tactics by sharing engaging and informative content with their customer base.

My partner and I started the company in August 2021.

WHAT KIND OF DESIGN WORK DOES ASHBI CREATIVE OFFER, ARE THE CLIENTS MOSTLY BUSINESSES OR INDIVIDUALS?

We offer a number of design and marketing services for our clientele. Most businesses we work with make use of all our Branding, Graphic, and Web Design services. After we complete the design work, we start marketing by way of email, content, social media, and search engine marketing, along with paid advertising campaigns.

AS A WEB DEVELOPER, WHAT ARE SOME OF THE TOOLS YOU USE TO SECURE THE WEBSITE AND ENSURE USER PRIVACY?

As a web developer, I use WordPress because of the extra security controls that ensure the security of my website and ensure user privacy. Some of these include:

  • Cloudflare’s free service allows me to monitor websites for malicious activity, as well as protect against DDoS attacks and other forms of online threats. Honeypot techniques catch bots and other hackers by baiting them into website inputs that are visible to bots but not to real humans. Once these bots trigger the honeypot, the software will know it’s not a real human.
  • Recaptcha3 anti-bot system prevents bots from accessing sensitive information or the website’s database. Real human visitors are free to use the site without friction, while bots will be stopped.
  • I ensure all automatic updates are ON, including WordPress, plugins, and themes, so that hackers cannot exploit any vulnerabilities in outdated versions, which could lead them to gain unauthorized access to the website.
  • It’s important to find a website host that provides extra WordPress security. These tools can disable parts of WordPress that are not needed or can be disabled most of the time. This minimizes the risk of being hacked while using WordPress.

    • WHAT ARE THE MAIN TYPES OF CYBERATTACKS THAT FOCUS ON SMALL AND MEDIUM-SIZED BUSINESS WEBSITES?

    The main types of cyberattacks that focus on small and medium-sized business websites are brute-force attacks, SQL injection attacks, and ransomware.

    Brute-force attacks are when hackers try every possible combination of letters and numbers to break into a website’s password.SQL injection attacks are when malicious code is injected into a website’s database to gain access to sensitive information.

    Ransomware is malware that encrypts all of your files and then holds them hostage until you pay the hacker a ransom fee.

    DO YOU HAVE ANY TIPS OR STRATEGIES FOR BUSINESSES TO PROTECT THEIR WEBSITES FROM HACKERS?

    The best way to protect your website from hackers is to make sure that the site is running on the latest version of the software, which will have the latest security updates. If you’re using a platform like WordPress, this means keeping track of what version it’s running and updating it whenever there’s an update available.

    The other way to protect your website from hackers is with Cloudflare. It works by acting as a proxy for your website, so if someone tries to hack into your site, Cloudflare will block them before they can get through.

    You should also be sure to run regular tests on your website, including penetration testing and vulnerability scanning. These tests will show you if there are any vulnerabilities in your site’s code that could allow hackers access to sensitive information or other attacks.

    Always keep offsite daily backups of your website. If anything goes wrong, you can deploy the full site to a new server.

    IF A WEBSITE IS HACKED, WHAT IS THE BEST WAY TO REGAIN CONTROL OF THE SITE?

    If your website is hacked, the best way to regain control of it is to have a full backup of your site always ready to deploy to a new server. You can do this by keeping your passwords different on your website, domain provider, and hosting.

    If your server is held hostage, you can notify your hosting, get a new server and deploy the website. If you keep your domain provider and hosting separate from your website, you can simply log in to your unaffected domain provider and point the DNS to the new server that is in your control.

    SHAULI ZACKS

    PUBLISHED ON: October 10, 2022

    ABOUT THE AUTHOR

    Shauli Zacks is a tech enthusiast who has reviewed and compared hundreds of programs in multiple niches, including cybersecurity, office and productivity tools, and parental control apps. He enjoys researching and understanding what features are important to the people using these tools.

article:closing-graphic-design-sales-cal.label: How to Close Graphic Design Sales Calls: Tips and Strategies for Maximum Success

content.title: How to run a useful design sales call
content.summary: Ask about the project, assess whether you can help and agree a clear next step before writing a proposal.
content.body:
A first design call should help both sides decide whether to work together. The aim is to understand the project well enough to suggest a next step. A persuasive pitch cannot replace a clear brief or a realistic scope.

Ask what prompted the enquiry

Find out why the client is looking for help now. What has changed in the business? What is difficult about the current brand, packaging or website? Ask for examples rather than assuming you already understand the problem.

Understand the work and the people involved

Discuss what already exists, which materials need to change and who will contribute feedback. Identify who approves the work and whether suppliers or other teams are involved. These details affect the scope and review process.

Talk about timing and budget

Ask about any launch date, dependencies and the budget available for the project. Explain what you need to assess before committing to a schedule or fee. If the requirements do not fit, discuss a smaller scope or say clearly that you may not be the right partner.

Show relevant work

Choose an example that relates to the client’s problem. Explain your contribution and the design decisions. Keep measured business results separate from design intentions, and avoid promising that another client will get the same outcome.

Agree the next step

Recap the problem, likely deliverables and open questions. Confirm whether you will prepare a proposal, need more information or recommend another route. The client should know what happens next and what you need from them.

Follow up with the details

Send a concise summary and the agreed next action. A proposal should describe the work, responsibilities, review stages, timing and fee. Make room for questions before either side commits.

article:envato-elements-must-have-graphi.label: How Envato Elements Fits a Design Project

content.title: How Envato Elements Fits a Design Project
content.summary: How to evaluate stock assets, check their fit with a brand system and keep a record of the licence before using them in client work.
content.body:
Asset libraries such as Envato Elements can provide photography, graphics, templates and other production materials. The useful question is not how many files are available. It is whether a particular asset helps the project without making the brand look interchangeable.

Start with the job the asset needs to do

Define the format, audience and message first. A stock photograph may help explain a service, while a template may speed up a temporary presentation. Neither should silently replace the visual decisions that make a brand recognisable.

Check the source files and rights

Review the item itself, any bundled documentation and the current licence before use. Envato says its subscription items receive a project-specific licence when downloaded, and a separate licence is needed for a different project. Its guidance also notes that preview content inside an item may come from other sources. Keep the item page and licence record with the project files so the team can check what was used later.

Test it in the actual design

  • Does the asset fit the brand’s type, colour and image direction?
  • Can it be cropped and reproduced at the sizes the project needs?
  • Will customers mistake a generic stock scene for a real product, team member or result?
  • Can the client maintain or replace it after handoff?

For pricing, availability and permitted uses, consult Envato’s current licence introduction and download guidance.

article:starting-a-graphic-design-busine.label: From Novice to Pro: How to Start a Thriving Graphic Design Business with No Prior Experience

content.title: Starting a graphic design business: the first decisions
content.summary: Define the work you can deliver, build an honest portfolio and establish a clear process for client projects.
content.body:
Starting a design studio means deciding what work you can deliver and how you will work with clients. A name and a website are useful, but they need to reflect a service you can explain and carry through to completion.

Choose a service you can deliver

Start with the skills and experience you have. Define the kind of project you can take on, the deliverables and any work that needs another specialist. If you are still learning, allow time for practice and feedback before promising client work.

Build an honest portfolio

Show projects that relate to the service you offer. Explain the brief, your role and the decisions behind the design. Label concepts and self-initiated work clearly. Ask permission before publishing client work or information that is not already public.

Set up a project process

Decide how you will gather information, agree the scope, present work and collect feedback. Confirm who approves each stage. Document the final files or access you will provide so the client knows what to expect at handoff.

Understand the time the work takes

Track research, design, revisions, meetings and administration. Use that information when planning a project and discussing its scope. Different deliverables and review requirements need different amounts of time.

Make your own website clear

Explain what you do, show relevant work and give visitors a way to enquire. Keep the language specific enough for a prospective client to recognise whether you can help. A small, accurate portfolio is more useful than a long list of services you cannot yet deliver.

Learn from completed projects

Review what went well, where the brief changed and what the client needed at handoff. Improve the process before taking on more work. A studio develops through its projects, relationships and the quality of the work it can consistently deliver.

article:prepare-for-a-shopify-redesign.label: What to prepare before a Shopify redesign

content.title: What to prepare before a Shopify redesign
content.summary: A useful redesign brief starts with products, customer questions and the parts of your store that need to keep working.
content.body:
Before choosing a new look, write down what customers need to do in your store. Finding a flavour, comparing sizes and understanding a delivery restriction are different design problems. Naming them gives the project a practical starting point.

Bring the catalogue, not just inspiration

Share your product list, variants, collection structure and available photography. Flag incomplete descriptions and any products that need a different page layout. A design made around three neat sample products can fall apart when the full range arrives.

Separate friction from preference

Keep two lists: things customers struggle with, and things your team wants to change visually. Support the first with customer questions, support tickets or observations where available. This helps decide which changes belong in the first release.

Make a list of what must survive

  • Existing URLs and the pages they should lead to.
  • Subscriptions, reviews and other app-dependent features.
  • Shipping, tax and fulfilment requirements.
  • Content your team needs to update without a designer.

Agree what “ready” means

Choose the journeys to review before launch: finding a product, selecting a variant, adding it to the cart and reaching checkout. Include a phone in that review. Confirm who supplies content and who approves the final store.

Chef Tanya’s Kitchen is a useful design example: the shop groups colourful product cards into one consistent browsing layout. Your store’s structure should come from your own catalogue and buying decisions.

article:what-a-creative-partnership-can-.label: What a monthly creative partnership can handle

content.title: What monthly creative support can do for your brand
content.shortTitle: A partner for the next piece
content.summary: How to organise recurring creative work, set priorities and recognise when a request needs its own project scope.
content.body:
A creative partnership is most useful when your team has a steady stream of work and an established direction. The value comes from continuity: the next email graphic, sales sheet or website update builds on decisions already made.

Start with the actual queue

List the next month’s deliverables, including sizes, channels, content owners and deadlines. “Social content” is too broad to estimate; a defined set of graphics using approved copy gives everyone a clearer task.

Choose one shared order of work

Give each request a priority and one person responsible for gathering feedback. When a new urgent item arrives, decide what moves back. Monthly capacity is a planning boundary, not a promise that every request can happen at once.

Separate creation from production

Adapting an approved design into several sizes is different from developing a new campaign direction. Label those tasks separately so the time goes toward the decisions that need it. Copywriting, email automation and media buying should only be assumed when they are explicitly in scope.

Two Ashbi examples show why the distinction matters. The HTY Foods Thanksgiving email arranges a seasonal offer and featured product into a campaign layout. Kalm College Circle’s sticker and name-tag sheet is production artwork based on an established direction. Each format needs different inputs and review, so identify the kind of task before assigning monthly capacity.

Use a project for a bigger change

A new identity or substantial website build needs its own milestones and review stages. Discuss whether to scope it separately before letting it consume the recurring queue.

  • Bring a prioritised list of upcoming work.
  • Identify who provides copy and assets.
  • Agree feedback and approval responsibilities.
  • Confirm capacity, timing and commercial terms in the proposal.

article:packaging-design-project-checkli.label: What your packaging designer needs before starting

content.title: Packaging design checklist: what your designer needs
content.summary: The product, supplier and content decisions that give packaging design a clear starting point.
content.body:
A pack has to fit a physical format and explain a product. A strong brief connects those two jobs before visual exploration begins.

Confirm the format with your supplier

Bring the current dieline, dimensions, material and print specifications. Identify who will answer production questions. A mockup is useful for reviewing a direction, but it does not replace a supplier-approved production file or proof.

Map the whole range

List products, variants and sizes, including likely near-term additions. Decide what stays consistent and what must differ. In CocoFro’s range, flavour colours change while the identity holds the family together.

Get product information into one document

  • Approved product names and descriptions.
  • Final copy and required label information supplied by your team.
  • Barcode assets and placement requirements.
  • Brand files, photography and existing pack examples.

Nominate the person who approves product information. Design review and specialist label review are separate responsibilities; agree both before print preparation.

Plan the handoff

Confirm which formats and variants are included, who checks supplier proofs and which files your team needs. Show how the pack will appear in a store or online listing as part of the review, without treating a presentation render as a finished production sample.

article:brand-refresh-or-rebrand.label: Brand refresh or full rebrand: how to choose

content.title: Brand refresh or full rebrand: how to choose
content.summary: Start with what has changed in the business, then decide how much of the identity needs to change with it.
content.body:
A tired-looking presentation does not always call for a new identity. Before starting, separate problems with the brand direction from problems with how it is being applied.

Identify what still works

List the elements customers recognise: a name, a colour, a pack shape or a distinctive mark. Bring examples of the identity working well alongside the pieces that feel inconsistent. That comparison can reveal whether clearer rules would solve the problem.

Ask what changed

A new audience, a different product range or a shift in positioning may require a deeper rethink. A growing collection of mismatched materials may instead need a focused refresh and a more usable system.

Define the decision before the deliverables

  • What should people understand about the business?
  • Which familiar elements should be retained?
  • Where does the identity need to work next?
  • Who approves the direction and supplies feedback?

Budget for the applications

Changing a logo affects more than the logo file. Map the website, packaging, sales materials and recurring content that need to follow. Agree a practical rollout so old and new materials do not compete indefinitely.

A useful first conversation should end with a clearer choice: improve consistency, refresh selected elements or develop a new direction. The scope follows that choice.
